Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 1:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat al-Anbiya' (The Prophets)

It is Meccan. Ibn Mas'ud said: "Surat Bani Isra'il, al-Kahf, Maryam, Ta-Ha and al-Anbiya' are among the first of my old (ʿitāq al-awwal) and they are of my ancient possessions (tilad)."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The reckoning of mankind has drawn near to them﴾. His saying ﴿has drawn near﴾ (iqtaraba) is of the form ifta'ala, from al-qurb (nearness). His saying ﴿for mankind, their reckoning﴾ means: the time of their reckoning. It is also said: their punishment. It is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever is subjected to scrutiny in the reckoning will be punished." The verse refers to the polytheists, not the believers; this is the view of some of them. He called the Hour "near" only because it is certain to come, and whatever is certain to come is near. Also, what remains of the world, compared with what has passed, is (little), so he called the Hour near in this sense. It has been narrated that when this verse was revealed, the polytheists desisted from some of what they were doing, but then, when they saw no sign of the Resurrection, they went back to their former pursuits. The same is narrated concerning His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾. And Allah knows best.

His saying ﴿while they are heedless, turning away﴾ means: they are heedless and turning away. It is also said: they are occupied with falsehood, away from the truth. It is said: they are heedless of what is intended for them, while they are intended by it.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 2:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There does not come to them any new reminder from their Lord﴾. The Mu'tazilites used this verse as evidence that the Qur'an is created (makhluq), and they said: everything that is muhdath (originated, newly come into being) is created. The answer to this is that the meaning of His saying ﴿muhdath﴾ is: muhdath in its revelation (tanzilih, its sending down), as mentioned by al-Azhari and others. It is said: it was sent down at one time after another time. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "Every time He renewed a reminder for them, they remained upon their ignorance." And al-Naqqash mentioned in his tafsir that the muhdath reminder here is what the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned and explained of the sunan (prophetic traditions), the admonitions and the proofs, apart from what is in the Qur'an; and it was attributed to the Lord because he said it by the command of the Lord, exalted is He.

And His saying: ﴿except that they listen to it while they are playing﴾, meaning: they listen to it while being playful (la'ibin).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 3:

And His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Their hearts are heedless﴾ meaning: unmindful; and it was said: occupied with falsehood away from the truth. Imru' al-Qays said:

(So like you, a pregnant woman has come to me at night, and a nursing one, and I distracted her from a child with amulets, still unweaned.)

That is, I occupied her.

And His saying: ﴿And they conceal the private conversation﴾ has two interpretations: one of them: they hid the private conversation; and the other: they revealed the private conversation. The Arabs say: asarra when he concealed, and asarra when he revealed. Some of the philologists said: asarra with the unpointed sin (س) means he concealed, and ashsharra with the pointed shin (ش) means he revealed. The poet said:

(When al-Hajjaj saw the drawing of his sword, the Kharijite who had been concealing [it] revealed [it].)

And His saying: ﴿Those who did wrong﴾ means: those who associated partners [with God].

And His saying: ﴿Is this not but a human being like you?﴾ They denied the sending of a human being, and they demanded the sending of angels.

And His saying: ﴿Will you then submit to magic while you see?﴾ means: you attend the magic and accept it.

And His saying: ﴿while you see﴾ means: you know that it is magic.

Almighty God's words: ﴿He said: My Lord knows every word in the heavens and the earth﴾. That is, the word is said secretly and said openly, in the heavens and the earth.

And His words: ﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ — its meaning is clear.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 5:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nay, they say: "A confusion of dreams"﴾, meaning: a jumble of dreams (tahawil ahlam). It is also said: a mixture of dreams (akhlat ahlam). It is also said: that which has neither interpretation (ta'wil) nor explanation (tafsir).

The poet said:

(Tales [Ṭasm] or a mirage in a valley, shimmering for the traveler at night, and the confused dreams of a dreamer.)

His saying: ﴿Nay, he has invented it﴾, meaning: he has fabricated it (ikhtalaqahu).

His saying: ﴿Nay, he is a poet﴾, meaning: like Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt and those who resemble him. The purpose of the verse is to show the contradiction in their statements and that they were not settled upon one thing.

His saying: ﴿So let him bring us a sign, as the earlier ones were sent with signs﴾, meaning: they demanded a sign like the she-camel, or the staff of Moses, and the hand of Moses, and what is similar to that. God, exalted is He, had already shown signs other than what they demanded.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 6:

Allah's saying: ﴿Not one town that We destroyed before them believed.﴾ Its meaning: not one people of a town who asked for a sign and were given it had believed before them. That is, We gave them the sign, and they did not believe. And His saying: ﴿We destroyed it﴾ means: We decreed its destruction.

And His saying: ﴿Will they then believe?﴾ Its meaning: just as those did not believe, so these will not believe.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 7:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We sent not before you except men to whom We revealed⁠ ⁠—﴾ meaning: We did not send angels before you to the earlier peoples, so that We would send an angel to your people.

And His saying: ﴿So ask the people of the reminder⁠ ⁠—﴾ Most of the scholars hold that what is meant by "the people of the reminder" (ahl al-dhikr) are the believers among the People of the Book. It is reported from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, that they are the scholars of this Ummah.

And His saying: ﴿if you do not know⁠ ⁠—﴾ its meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 8:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We did not make them bodies﴾, meaning: possessing bodies.

And His words: ﴿that do not eat food﴾ are clear. And His words: ﴿nor were they immortal﴾, meaning: in this world. This is a refutation of their saying: ﴿And they said, "What is this Messenger that eats food and walks in the markets?"﴾ and so on.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 9:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then We fulfilled the promise to them﴾. Its meaning: We fulfilled to them the promise regarding punishment and reward.

And His saying: ﴿So We saved them, and whom We willed, and We destroyed the transgressors﴾. That is: We saved the believers and We destroyed the deniers, and every denier is a polytheist and a transgressor against himself. Al-sarf (excess, transgression) is going beyond the limit.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 10:

And His Exalted saying: ﴿Indeed We have sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder﴾. Regarding it there are several opinions. The first: "your reminder" means "your talk" (ḥadīthakum). It was also said: "your reminder" means "that which you need of your religion." Mujahid said: "your reminder" means "your honour," and it is an honour for the one who believes in it, not for the one who disbelieves in it.

And His saying: ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ means: "Will you not then take heed?"

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 11:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And how many a town have We broken (qasamna)﴾. Qasm (al-qasm) means breaking, and fasm, with the letter fa', means splitting (al-sad'). In the report: "The people of the high ranks will be raised to a chamber of pearl in which there is no qasm and no fasm."

And His words: ﴿a town whose people were wrongdoers (zalimah)﴾, meaning: its people had done wrong.

And His words: ﴿and We brought into being after them another people (qawman akharin)﴾, meaning: another group (fariqan akharin).

**Where the Quran says ﴿So when they perceived Our punishment﴾**, it means: (they found Our punishment). It is also said: Our punishment reached them.

**Where the Quran says ﴿at once they were fleeing from it in haste﴾**, it means: they were fleeing at a run. It is said: "rakada al-dabbah" (he spurred the animal) when he made it quicken its pace.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 13:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do not flee in haste﴾, meaning: do not run away.

And His saying: ﴿and return to that in which you were given luxury﴾, meaning: in which you were made comfortable. The mutraf (one given luxury) is the one who is bestowed with favours. It is also said: "to your worldly life," ﴿and your dwellings﴾ in which you were made comfortable. Most of the people of tafsir (exegesis) said: these verses were revealed concerning the people of a city who disbelieved, so Allah gave power over them to some tyrants. It is also said that this was Bukhtnasr (Nebuchadnezzar). When the torment of the sword struck them, they fled. The angels said to them, while the swords had already seized them: "Do not flee, and return to that in which you were given luxury and your dwellings." ﴿That perhaps you may be questioned﴾ about your worldly life, so that you would be given what you wish and denied whom you wish. They said this to them in mockery. It has also been said that this concerns the people of a city upon whom a torment from the sky befell, so they went out fleeing, and the angels said this to them. It is also said concerning His saying ﴿that perhaps you may be questioned﴾, meaning: you will be asked why you abandoned what would set right your religion and the affair of your Hereafter, and occupied yourselves with what brings punishment upon you. It is also said: "that perhaps you may be questioned" about what you witnessed of the punishment. The angels said this as a rebuke to them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis) al-Qur'an) on surah 21, verse 14:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed, we were wrongdoers."﴾ Al-wayl (الويل) is a supplication for destruction.

And His saying: ﴿wrongdoers﴾ means wrongdoers against ourselves.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 15:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So that remained their cry⦆ — i.e., their supplication and their saying.

And His saying: ﴿until We made them as a harvest, extinguished﴾ — al-hasid (the harvested crop) is that which has been uprooted entirely.

And His saying: ﴿extinguished﴾ — i.e., dead. The meaning of the verse: We made them as though they had never been.
Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾ That is: for play.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 17:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Had We wished to take a pastime﴾. The scholars differed concerning the word lahw (pastime, diversion) here, on two views. The first: that lahw is the woman (wife). The second: that lahw is the child (offspring). The first is more apparent, for intercourse is called lahw in the Arabic language, and the woman is the place of intercourse. The poet said:

(Does Basbasa claim today that I have grown old, and that such as I no longer become pastime?)

And it is reported from some of them that lahw is singing, but this is weak in this context.

His saying: ﴿We would have taken it from Our presence﴾, i.e., We would have taken it from Our own presence, not from yours. It is also said: it means We would have taken it in a place where you do not see.

His saying: ﴿if We were ever to do it﴾, i.e., We would not have done it. It is also said: if We were doing it, and We did not do it, because it does not befit Us.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 18:

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Nay, We hurl the truth against falsehood﴾. The truth here is the saying of God, exalted is He: "Indeed, He has no son," and the falsehood is their saying that God has taken a son. It is also said that the truth is the Qur'an, and the falsehood is Satan.

His saying: ﴿hurl﴾ means: We cast.

His saying: ﴿so it destroys it﴾ means: it removes it. It is said: "I dumped (damagha) so-and-so," meaning I broke his skull (dimagh) and killed him.

His saying: ﴿and behold, it vanishes﴾ means: it departs. This is in terms of clarifying the proof and the argument, not in terms of eliminating disbelief entirely, for disbelief and falsehood in the world are abundant.

His saying: ﴿And woe to you for what you describe﴾. Qatada said: "for what you lie about." Al-Hasan said: "It is for every describer of falsehood until the Day of Resurrection."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 19:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: whoever is in the heavens and the earth, as servants and as possessions.

And His saying: ﴿And those who are with Him﴾, meaning: the angels.

And His saying: ﴿They do not consider themselves too proud to worship Him﴾. Meaning: they do not magnify themselves so as to refuse His worship. Ibn Faris mentioned in his tafsir, in a report: when God, may He be exalted, settled upon His Throne, an angel prostrated and did not raise his head from prostration until the Day of Resurrection. When he raises his head on the Day of Resurrection, he will say: "Glory be to You, I have not worshipped You as You deserve to be worshipped, except that I did not associate anything with You and did not take for You any equal."

And His saying: ﴿Nor do they tire﴾, meaning: they do not grow weary. It is said: "a beast is ḥasīrah" when it is weary (ʿayyah). Kaʿb al-Aḥbār said: "Glorifying (tasbīḥ) is for them like breathing is for the children of Adam."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 20:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They glorify Him night and day; they never tire﴾. It means: they glorify constantly, they do not weaken and they do not cease. Know that there is no night nor day for the angels; rather, what is meant by mentioning night and day here is constancy in glorifying (tasbih).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 21:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth who can raise the dead?﴾ The meaning of His words ﴿from the earth﴾ is: from wood and stone (and most of the idols of the polytheists were made of wood and stone), and both are from the earth.

And His words ﴿who can raise the dead﴾ mean: who can give life. Divinity is not deserved except by one who is able to give life and to create from non-existence, for that is the bestowing of blessings in their most eloquent forms, and this does not befit the description of a human being or of anything created. And they recited, from al-A'sha, on raising the dead:

(If you were to lean a dead man against its neck, he would live and not be moved to a grave,
until people say, from what they saw: "How wondrous, the dead man who rises!")

It is also recited as ﴿yunshirun﴾ with a fatha on the ya', meaning: they give life forever. The meaning of the verse is a rebuke against those who take idols as gods, and a clarification that divinity does not befit them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 22:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been ruined.﴾ Most of the people of tafsir (exegesis) said: "illa" (except) here means "ghayr" (other than). The poet said:

(And every brother who parts from his brother... by the life of your father, none remain except the two Farqads)

He means: other than the two Farqads. This is according to what they believed about the permanence of the heavens and the earth.

Some of them said: in ﴿except Allah﴾, "illa" here means "wa" (and). The meaning is: had there been in them gods, and Allah (also), they would both have been ruined. The meaning of corruption in the heavens and the earth, if the god were two, is the corruption of management and the disruption of affairs through the occurrence of dispute and opposition, and this is also the meaning of the words of the Most High: ﴿And some of them would have overpowered others.﴾

And His words: ﴿Glory be to Allah, Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.﴾ He declared Himself free of what the polytheists attribute to Him of partners and offspring.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 23:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾. It means: He is not questioned about what He decides concerning His creation, whereas the creatures are questioned about their deeds and actions. It was also said: He is not questioned about what He does, because all of it is wisdom and rightness, whereas they will be questioned about what they do, since error is possible for them. It was also said: the meaning of "He is not questioned about what He does" is: it is not said to Him, "Why?" or "For what reason?", unlike the case of creatures. In the verse there is a refutation of the Qadariyya (the Qadariyya, a early school that denied divine predestination of human acts), and a complete cutting off of their doubt.

Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali narrated that Imran ibn Husayn said to him: "Do you see what people strive for and toil at: is it a matter that has been decreed upon them, or a thing they are starting anew?" I said: "No, rather it is a matter that has been decreed upon them." He said: "Would it not then be injustice?" I said: "Glory be to God! ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾." He said to me: "You are right, Abu al-Aswad, and you have been granted understanding." Then Imran narrated that a man from Juhayna (or Muzayna) came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said to him: "Concerning what people do and toil at, is it a thing that has been decreed upon them, or a thing they are starting anew?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is a thing that has been decreed upon them." That man said: "O Messenger of God, would it not then be injustice?" He said: "No." Then he recited the words of Allah the Exalted: {He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned}. The Shaykh said: We have mentioned this report in the book "Musnad al-Qadr" (the Book of Predestination).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 24:

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Or have they taken gods besides Him? Say: Bring your proof.﴾ That is: your argument (hujjatakum).

And His saying: ﴿This is the reminder of those with me﴾ That is: the reminder of those with me concerning what they were commanded regarding the lawful (al-halal) and the unlawful (al-haram).

And His saying: ﴿And the reminder of those before me﴾ That is: of those among them who lived by obedience and perished by disobedience. And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The reminder of those with me is the Qur'an, and the reminder of those before me is the Torah and the Gospel." Its meaning is: Consult the Qur'an, the Torah, the Gospel and all the other books: do you find in them that God has taken a son?

And His saying: ﴿Nay, most of them do not know the truth, so they turn away﴾ its meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 25:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send any messenger before you except that We revealed to him that there is no deity except Me, so worship Me.﴾ Meaning: make Him one (wahhidun).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 26:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿And they say: The Most Merciful has taken to Himself a son.﴾ Qatadah said: A group of the polytheists said: Allah the Exalted has intermarried with the jinn, and so the angels are His daughters.

And His saying: ﴿Glory be to Him!﴾ He has declared Himself far exalted above what they say.

And His saying: ﴿Rather, they are honoured servants.﴾ That is: they are honoured slaves.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 21, verse 27:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾. This is a praise from God for the angels. The meaning of His saying ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾ is that they do not say anything contrary to it. This is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, do not put yourselves forward before God and His Messenger﴾, meaning: do not say anything contrary to the Book and the Sunnah. It has been established by the narration of ʿĀʾishah, may God be pleased with her, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever introduces into our religion something that is not part of it, it is rejected." And innovation (iḥdāth) in the religion (dīn) is to say something contrary to the Book and the Sunnah.

And His saying: ﴿and they act by His command﴾ means: they do not oppose Him, neither in speech nor in action. It is also said that its meaning is: when He commands them with a matter, they obey; so when He says to them, "Do," they say, "Obedience."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 28:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾, meaning: what they have put forward and what they have put off. It is also said: what is before them is the Hereafter, and what is behind them is their deeds.

And His saying: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾, its meaning: except for the one who says: "There is no god but Allah." It is also said: except for the one whose deed Allah approves.

And His saying: ﴿And they are fearful of His awe﴾, meaning: of His punishment.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 21, verse 29:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And whoever among them should say, "Indeed, I am a god besides Him," that one We would recompense with Hell. Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers.﴾

If it is said: Did any of the angels say, "Indeed, I am a god besides Him"? We say: its meaning is "if they had said it," though they did not say it. The well-known answer is that what is meant by it is Iblis, may Allah curse him, for he invited people to obey him. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿And whoever among them should say, "Indeed, I am a god"﴾. This is evidence that whoever calls a person to obey him in disobedience to the Creator, it is as if he had said: "Worship me," or "take me as a god."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 30:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Have not those who disbelieved seen that the heavens and the earth were a joined mass, and We separated them?﴾ If someone says: He said, "Have not the disbelievers seen," yet the disbelievers did not see any of this, nor did the Muslims! The answer to this is that its meaning is: "Have they not known through your informing them?" It has also been said: "Have they not been informed?" As for ratq (rataq, joined, sealed-up) in the language, it is al-sadd (blocking), and fatq (separation) is al-shaqq (splitting). The poet said:

(It is easy for them when they are angry... the anger of enemies and their humiliation)

(Sealing up the breaches and splitting the sealed, and undoing matters and fixing them)

As for the meaning of the verse: Ibn 'Abbas said: His words ﴿they were a joined mass﴾ mean that the heaven and the earth were stuck together, and We separated them with air. Others said: its meaning is that the heaven was one thing, and We split it and made it seven heavens, and the earth was one thing, and We split it and made it seven earths. The third view was stated by Mujahid: We split the heaven with rain and the earth with plants.

And His words: ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾. If someone says: Some living things have been created from other than water, so how is His saying ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾ correct? Also, a person may die by water, and trees and plants may perish by water? The answer is in two respects. First: water here is the sperm-drop (nutfah), and "living" refers to the human being, meaning: every living human being is from water. The second answer: this is stated in the sense of multiplicity, and most living beings on earth are created from water or their survival depends on water, so the meaning of the verse is correct in this respect.

His words: ﴿Will they not then believe?﴾ — its meaning is clear.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 31:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We placed firm mountains on the earth﴾, meaning: mountains that are fixed (thawabit). It was also said: heavy (thiqalan). The poet said:

(Its root is beneath the earth and its height... reaches to the star, a branch that cannot be attained, tall)

His saying: ﴿lest it should sway with them﴾, meaning: lest it sway with them. The mayd is movement (al-haraka).

His saying: ﴿And We placed in it broad paths, ways﴾, the fajj is the wide space between two mountains.

His saying: ﴿ways﴾, meaning: well-trodden roads (turuqan maslukah).

His saying: ﴿that they may be guided﴾, meaning: that they may be guided to the truth.

God's words: ﴿And We made the sky a protected ceiling﴾. That is, protected from falling upon the earth, which is the meaning of God's words: ﴿Indeed, God holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease [to move]﴾. It is also said that its meaning is: protected from the devils by shooting stars (shuhub).

And His words: ﴿Yet they turn away from its signs.﴾ Its signs: its sun, its moon, its stars, its height, its holding up without pillars, and other than that.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 33:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And it is He who created the night and the day, the sun and the moon﴾. What is known from Ibn ʿAbbas, through the transmission of ʿIkrimah, is that he said: Allah the Exalted created the night before the day. And he recited the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Have not those who disbelieved seen that the heavens and the earth were a joined mass, and We separated them?﴾ Meaning: they were dark, enclosed in a joined mass, and then they were parted by light.

And His words: ﴿And the sun and the moon, each in an orbit they swim﴾. Meaning: they run. It is said: an orbit (falak) carries them around, beneath the sky. It is also said: the sky carries them around, and Allah knows best. He mentioned ﴿they swim﴾ (yasbahun) and did not say "it swims" (yasbahu), as is said of non-rational things, because He ascribed to them what is ascribed to rational beings, namely running and swimming, so He used the form for rational beings.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 34:

The words of the Most High: ﴿We did not grant to any human before you immortality﴾. They used to say: "We await for Muhammad the vicissitudes of fate (rayb al-manun)." So the Most High said: ﴿We did not grant to any human before you immortality﴾, meaning: death is a known, well-trodden path, unavoidable for every living being.

And His words: ﴿So if you die, will they be the immortals?﴾ Its meaning: will they be the immortals if you die?

It has been narrated that when the Prophet (ﷺ) passed away, Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) entered, placed his mouth between his eyes, and put his hand on the side of his head, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, you were good in life and in death." Then he recited the words of the Most High: ﴿We did not grant to any human before you immortality. So if you die, will they be the immortals?﴾ Umar used to say: "He has not died." When Abu Bakr recited this verse, it was as if the people had not heard this verse until that moment, and they turned away from Umar's statement and knew that he had died.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 35:

The Most High's saying: ﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾. We have explained this before.

And His saying: ﴿And We test you with evil and good﴾, that is: with ease and hardship, health and sickness, with misery and happiness, and other things that vary for a human being. It was also said: "with evil and good" means with what they love and what they dislike. And it is said: evil is the dominance of desire over a person, and good is protection from sins (ʿişma). This was said by Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah.

And His saying: ﴿a trial﴾, that is: a tribulation and a test.

And His saying: ﴿And to Us you will be returned﴾, that is: you will be brought back.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 36:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when those who disbelieve see you, they take you not except in ridicule﴾, meaning: they do not take you except in ridicule.

And His words: ﴿Is this the one who mentions your gods?﴾, meaning: who disparages your gods. It is said: "So-and-so mentions so-and-so," meaning he disparages him; and "So-and-so mentions Allah," meaning he magnifies Him and honours Him.

And His words: ﴿while they, at the mention of the Most Merciful, are disbelievers﴾. He said this because they used to say: "We do not know the Most Merciful except Musaylimah." And "they" (hum) is the second (pronoun), serving as a connective (silah).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 37:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾. Concerning this there are several opinions. The first: it means hastiness and haste. "Man" (al-insan) here is Adam, may God's blessings be upon him, and God created him without the sequence by which the rest of the children of Adam are created from a drop (nutfah), a clinging clot (alaqah), a lump of flesh (mudghah), and so on. This is a good opinion. The second opinion: "of haste" means "hasty," i.e., he is hasty (ajulan), and it is permissible that "man" refers to all the children of Adam. As for Ibn 'Abbas, he said: it is Adam, when God breathed the spirit into him and it reached his chest, he wanted to stand up, and that was his haste. Al-Kalbi mentioned that when the spirit was breathed into him, he looked at the sun and saw that it was setting, so he said: "O God, complete my creation before the sun sets," and that was his haste. The third opinion: "man was created and haste is of him," and it was said: "and haste is in him." This is in the manner of hyperbole, as the Arabs say of a wicked person, "he was created from evil," and likewise they say, "so-and-so was created from good," when mentioned in the manner of hyperbole.

The fourth opinion: His saying ﴿Man was created of haste﴾ means "of clay (tin)." The poet said:

(The acacia in the hard rock is its place of growth... and the palm grows between water and clay ('ajal))

That is, clay (al-tin).

As for His saying ﴿I will show you My signs, so do not seek to hasten [them]﴾, this is concerning the polytheists, for they used to seek to hasten the Hour, as God said in another place: ﴿Those who do not believe in it seek to hasten it﴾. Some of them said: ﴿My signs﴾ means "My promises." His saying ﴿so do not seek to hasten﴾ means: do not ask Me for the punishment before its time. This verse was revealed because al-Nadr ibn al-Harith had said: "O God, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment."
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they say, "When will this promise be fulfilled, if you are truthful?"﴾ Its meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 39:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If only those who disbelieved would know the time when they will not be able to ward off﴾, i.e., they will not be able to repel [the fire].

And His saying: ﴿the Fire from their faces, nor from their backs﴾, its meaning is apparent.

And His saying: (nor will they be given help). I.e., they will not be prevented from the punishment. In the verse there is an omitted response (jawab maHdhuf), and its meaning is: they would know the truth of Our promise.

And His saying: ﴿If only ... would know﴾ at the beginning of the verse, its meaning is: if only they would see.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 40:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Rather, it will come upon them suddenly﴾, meaning: the Resurrection will come upon them unexpectedly.

And His words: ﴿and it will confound them﴾, meaning: it will bewilder them. It is said: "So-and-so is mabhut," meaning: bewildered, and this is the meaning of the words of the Exalted: ﴿So the one who disbelieved was confounded﴾.

And His words: ﴿so they will not be able to avert it, nor will they be given respite﴾, meaning: they will not be given time (yumhalun).

"His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And mockery was certainly made of messengers before you﴾ — its meaning is apparent.

And His saying: ﴿So there descended upon those who mocked among them﴾ — i.e., there descended upon those who mocked them. ﴿That which they used to ridicule.﴾ — i.e., the requital of their mockery."

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Who protects you by night and by day from the Most Merciful?﴾ That is: who guards you. The poet said:

(Indeed Sulaymá, may Allah protect her... she withheld something that would not harm her)

And His saying: ﴿by night and by day from the Most Merciful﴾ means: from the punishment of the Most Merciful, and Allah, Exalted is He, protects His servants from the punishment of His own self.

And His saying: ﴿Nay, but they turn away from the remembrance of their Lord﴾ — its meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 43:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Or do they have gods that can protect them from Us?﴾ meaning: that can protect them from the punishment, apart from Us.

And His words: ﴿They are unable to help themselves﴾ meaning: to defend themselves.

And His words: ﴿Nor can they be given companionship from Us﴾ meaning: they cannot be granted protection (ijarah). It is said: "God grant you protection (ajaraka Allah)," meaning: may God preserve you. The Arabs say: "ṣaḥabaka Allah," meaning: may God preserve and help you. It has also been said: "yuṣḥabūn" means: they will be helped.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 44:

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Nay, We gave good things to these people and their fathers﴾ means: We gave them respite and reprieve. It is also said: "We gave them good things" means: We gave them blessing.

His saying: ﴿Until a long time passed over them﴾ means: the period of time extended over them.

His saying: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outskirts?﴾ Most of the scholars hold that this is the rise (ẓuhūr) of the Prophet, and his conquest of the abodes of polytheism, land by land and town by town. The evidence for the soundness of this interpretation is that He said: ﴿Are they then the victors?﴾, meaning: victory does not belong to them; rather, victory belongs to Me and to My Messenger. Ibn Jurayj narrated: "What is reduced from all the other lands is added to the Levant (al-Sham), and what is reduced from the Levant is added to the land of Palestine, and the place of gathering (al-mahshar) is there." ʿIkrimah said: "If the land were reduced, no one would find a place to sit in it." Rather, the intended meaning of the verse is the passing away of its best people and its scholars. It is also said: it is the death of its inhabitants. And it has been said: it is its ruin.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 45:

His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿Say: I only warn you by revelation﴾, meaning: by the Qur'an.

And His saying: ﴿And the deaf do not hear the call﴾. It is also read: "lā yasmaʿu al-ṣumm al-duʿāʾ" (the deaf do not hear the call), with the verb in the third person masculine. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Muqriʾ read: "lā tasmaʿu al-ṣumm al-duʿāʾ" (you do not make the deaf hear the call), with the verb in the second person feminine. As for the well-known reading, its meaning is apparent. The deaf (al-ṣumm) are the disbelievers, and He called them deaf because they did not hear what would benefit them.

And His saying: ﴿When they are warned﴾, meaning: when they are warned (yukhawwafūn) by revelation.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 46:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And if a breath of your Lord's punishment should touch them﴾. The nafha (a light, brief blow or puff) is the slight push; the Arabs say, "Fulan struck (nafaha) with the sword," in this sense, and it is different from... The nafkha (a blast) must involve the escape of wind from fear. The meaning of ﴿And if a breath of your Lord's punishment should touch them﴾ is: a portion of your Lord's punishment. It was also said: the least thing of your Lord's punishment.

And His words: ﴿They will surely say, "Woe to us! Indeed, we were wrongdoers."﴾ Its meaning: "O our destruction, indeed we were polytheists," as if they acknowledged against themselves that they deserved the punishment.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 21, verse 47:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We shall set up the scales of justice﴾ means: possessors of justice. And qist (قسط) means justice (ʿadl). In what is well known among the reports: the scale has a tongue and two pans. And in some transmitted reports: Dawud, peace be upon him, said: "O Lord, show me the scale by which the deeds of the servants are weighed," so He showed it to him. ﴿The scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in anything; and even if it is the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it forth﴾. Each of its pans is like the distance between the east and the west. He said: "O Lord, who will fill this with good deeds?" He said: "O Dawud, when I am pleased with My servant, I fill it for him with a morsel or a date." And God knows best.

As for how the weighing takes place, some have said that good deeds and bad deeds are weighed. It was also said that the final outcomes of deeds are weighed. Some said: the scale is a sign by which the measures of deserving reward and punishment are known. The correct view is that the scale is real in fact. If it is said: He said elsewhere, ﴿So We shall not set up for them on the Day of Resurrection any weight﴾, how is the reconciliation between the two verses? The answer: the meaning of His saying ﴿So We shall not set up for them on the Day of Resurrection any weight﴾ is that their weighing will not be upright according to the truth, for their scale is deficient, lacking and light. It is also said: ﴿So We shall not set up for them on the Day of Resurrection any weight﴾ means reward. Some of the Kharijites said concerning the striking of Ibn Muljam against ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him:

(O blow of one who is pious, he intended by it only / to attain, from the Lord of the Throne, good pleasure)

(Indeed I remember a day and I reckon it / the most complete of creatures before Allah in weight)

That is, in reward. We disavow the meaning of this poetry and its speaker.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So no soul will be wronged in anything﴾ means: nothing is added to its bad deeds, nor is anything subtracted from its good deeds.

His saying: ﴿Even if it is the weight of a mustard seed﴾ means: the weight of a grain of mustard.

His saying: ﴿We will bring it forth﴾ means: We will produce it, in order to requite for it.

It was read in the irregular (shadhdh) reading: "ātaynā bihā" with a long alif, from ītāʾ (giving), meaning: We will requite by it, or We will give by it.

His saying: ﴿And sufficient is We as reckoners﴾ means: as those who call to account. It was also said: as guardians, knowing; and it was said: as counters.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 48:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave Moses and Aaron the Furqan﴾. Regarding it there are two opinions. The first: it is the Tawrah (Torah). The second: it is the proof (burhan) by which Moses's truth was distinguished from the falsehood of Pharaoh.

And His saying: ﴿and a light﴾. It has been recited without the conjunction waw. With the waw, it is another attribute of the Tawrah, if we take al-Furqan to mean the Tawrah. If we take al-Furqan to mean the proof, then the meaning is: We gave him the proof, and We gave him the Tawrah which is a light. Without the waw, the meaning of al-Furqan on this reading is only the Tawrah, and His saying ﴿and a light﴾ is an attribute of it.

And His saying: ﴿and a reminder for the God-fearing﴾, that is: an admonition (tadhkir) for the God-fearing (al-Muttaqun).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 49:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who fear their Lord in the unseen﴾. He said ﴿in the unseen﴾ because the believers fear Him while they do not see Him, whereas He sees them and they are not unseen to Him. And His saying: ﴿and they are apprehensive of the Hour﴾, that is: fearful.

This is the commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on Surah 21, verse 50.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And this is a blessed reminder which We have sent down.﴾ The meaning of "blessed" (mubarak) has already been explained. It is also said that it is sought for blessing (yutabarak bihi), meaning: good is sought from it.

As for His saying: ﴿Will you then deny it?﴾ it is mentioned in the form of rebuke and reproach for their denial.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 51:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We indeed gave Ibrahim his guidance before [this], and We were of him well-knowing﴾. Regarding "rushd" (guidance, right conduct) there are two opinions: the first is that it is guidance (al-hidayah), and the second is that it is prophethood (al-nubuwwah).

As for His saying ﴿before [this]﴾, there are two opinions. The first is: before puberty (al-bulugh), that is, when he came out of the cave while he was young, and he looked at the stars, the sun and the moon and reasoned by inference, as we mentioned in Surah al-An'am. The second opinion is: before [the time of] Musa and Harun.

As for His saying ﴿and We were of him well-knowing﴾, that means: knowing (arifin).
When He said to his father and his people, "What are these statues to which you are devoted?" — that is, the idols to which you are persistently attached in worship.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 53:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said: "We found our fathers worshipping them."﴾ Its meaning: we found them doing so, and so we followed them.
Allah's saying: ﴿He said, "Indeed you and your fathers have been in clear error."﴾ That is: in manifest error. Al-bayn means the evident, and al-mubin means the one that makes clear.
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They said, "Have you come to us with the truth, or are you among the jesters?"﴾ That is: with what is true and in earnest, or are you among those who mock?

Almost identical to the surah 21 verse 56 quotation: the Qur'anic quotations are to be kept with ﴿ ﴾ markers and translated plainly.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who originated them.﴾ Meaning: who created them.

And His saying: ﴿And I am of those who bear witness to that.﴾ Meaning: to the fact that He is the God who alone deserves worship, and that the idols are not gods. It was also said: "And I am among the witnesses that He is the Creator of the heavens and the earth."

"And by God, I will surely plot against your idols" (Qur'an 21:57).

Al-Kayd (plotting, scheming): bringing harm upon another by way of some kind of planning. It is also said that al-kayd resembles warfare (al-muharabah).

In the Maghazi of the Messenger (ﷺ) it is said: he raided such-and-such a place but did not meet any kayd, meaning, no fighting.

As for His words: "after you have turned away, retreating" (Qur'an 21:57), meaning: after you have gone off, retreating, to your festival. If it is asked: how can a plot against the idols be conceived, since they do not understand? We say: we will explain the manner in which he plotted against them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 58:

His words: ﴿So he reduced them to fragments﴾. It is recited as "judhadhan" (جذاذا) and "judhadhan" and in the irregular reading "judhadhan" (جذاذا). As for "judhadhan" with a raised vowel (الرفع), it is like "hutaman" (الحطام) and "rufat" (الرفات) [both meaning debris]. As for "judhadhan" with a kasra, it is the plural of "judhadh" (الجذيذ), like "khafif" and "khifaf" [light and light ones]. Its meaning is that he cut them and broke them, i.e., made them into pieces, piece by piece and fragment by fragment.

In the story: when they went out to their festival, they said to him: "Will you not come out with us?" He said: "No, I am sick," meaning: "I have not yet recovered." Then he said to himself: ﴿By God, I will certainly scheme against your idols﴾. A man among them heard him. They went off, and no one remained in the city. So he came to the house of their idols, carrying an axe. In the house there were seventy-two idols: some of stone, some of silver, some of gold, and other materials. The largest idol was of gold, adorned with jewels, its two eyes were blazing rubies, and it was in a great form. He took the axe and broke them all except the largest, which he left alone, and he hung the axe on its neck. It was also said that he tied it with his hand. This is the "scheme" of the idols, meaning: he schemed against them according to what they believed about them. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿So he reduced them to fragments, except a great one among them, that they might return to it﴾. Poetry was recited about "judhadh":

(He shattered the idols in their sanctuary... that was for God, the Most High, the Mighty.)

As for His words: ﴿that they might return to it﴾, there are two opinions. The first: "that they might return to it" means that they might return from polytheism to Him, i.e., at this act. The second opinion: "that they might return to the great one," meaning: when they saw the likenesses of the great idol cut and broken, and they knew that it was like them, and there was no defence from it, they would know that there was no defence from it either. As for the saying of one who said that the meaning of the verse, ﴿that they might return to it﴾, is that the great idol was the one who did that to them out of zeal and pride, this is a false opinion, because it does not enter any person's mind that the great idol would break the small idols. Rather, he hung the axe on the neck of the great one as a reproach and a rebuke to them. It was also said that it was by way of establishing the proof against them, for their belief necessitates this, namely that the great one would not be content with the small idols, were they to have reason.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They said, "Who has done this to our gods? Indeed, he is among the wrongdoers."﴾ There is an implied elision here: they returned and entered upon the idols, and when they saw them, they said so.

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, he is among the wrongdoers﴾ means: among the criminals (al-mujrimin).

"Their saying: ﴿We heard a young man mention them﴾, that is, a youth, ﴿who speaks of them﴾, that is, who blames them. And in the story, that man who was heard from had mentioned the scheming of the idols, and so he said this.

And His saying: ﴿who is called Abraham﴾ is well known."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 61:

Regarding His the Exalted's saying: ﴿They said, "Then bring him before the eyes of the people"﴾, in the account, the king, who was Nimrod, said this statement, and its meaning is: bring him into the sight of the people.

As for His saying: ﴿that perhaps they may bear witness﴾, there are two opinions concerning it. The first: that they may witness his punishment when we punish him. The other opinion: perhaps they may hear the man's statement that he said such-and-such about the idols. Al-Suddi said: the king disliked to punish him without clear evidence.
The words of the Most High: ﴿They said, "Is it you who did this to our gods, O Abraham?"﴾ They sought from him an admission and acknowledgment of what he had done.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 63:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Rather, it was done by this, their chief."﴾ Know that it has been established from the Prophet through the narration of Abu al-Zinad, from al-A'raj, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet said: "Ibrahim told three lies" — and in one narration: "concerning Allah" — his saying: ﴿Rather, it was done by this, their chief﴾, and his saying: ﴿Indeed, I am sick﴾, and his saying to Sarah: "This is my sister."

The Shaykh, the Imam, said: Abu 'Ali al-Shafi'i informed us of this hadith, saying: Abu al-Hasan ibn [Firas] said: Abu Ja'far al-Dibli related to us, saying: Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Makhzumi related to us, saying: Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah related to us, from Abu al-Zinad... the hadith.

The people of the meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: Ibrahim said what he said by permission from Allah, the Exalted, for the purpose of reform, and it is like what He permitted Yusuf to say to his brothers: "O caravan, indeed you are thieves." Some of them said: it is a statement whose wording differs from its meaning, and every statement has its interpretation. As for his saying: ﴿Rather, it was done by this, their chief﴾, meaning: according to your assumption and belief, and it is in the form of imposing the argument, as we have explained, in order to establish the report. Some of them said its meaning is: "Rather, it was done by this, their chief — ﴿so ask them, if they can speak﴾," said as a conditional. Al-Nahhas said: this interpretation is far-fetched, and it contradicts the established reports. As for his saying: ﴿Indeed, I am sick﴾, meaning: I will become sick. It was also said its meaning is: "sick," that is, distressed by your misguidance, so that he was as if sick at heart because of that. As for his saying to Sarah: "This is my sister," meaning: my sister in religion. The most preferable is the first meaning we mentioned, which is the view of the Sunni scholars (ahl al-sunnah), namely that Allah, the Exalted, permitted him to say it.

ۧ"Then they returned to themselves and said, 'Indeed, it is you who are the wrongdoers.'" Its meaning: they returned to their thinking and their reason, and said, "Indeed, it is you who are the wrongdoers," meaning: by your worshipping that which cannot ward off anything from itself.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 65:

The words of the Exalted, ﴿Then they were turned back on their heads﴾. The people of tafsir said: God, Exalted is He, caused the truth to run upon their tongues in the first statement, then wretchedness overtook them. This is the meaning of His words, ﴿Then they were turned back on their heads﴾. Its meaning is that they returned to their polytheism. It is also said: "The patient relapsed (nakasa al-mareedu)" when he returned to his former state. It was also said: "They were turned back on their heads" means they returned, and its meaning is: to arguing on behalf of the idols.

And His words, ﴿Indeed you know that these do not speak﴾. Its meaning is: then how can we ask them?

Almost there in my reasoning: the passage is short, so I translate it directly.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 66:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: Do you then worship, besides Allah, that which can neither benefit you at all nor harm you?﴾ Its meaning: it does not benefit you if you worship it, and it does not harm you if you abandon its worship.

And His saying, ﴿Uff to you!﴾ means: stench and filth upon you. And His saying, ﴿and what you worship besides Allah﴾ means: the idols.

And His saying, ﴿Will you not reason?﴾ means: Do you not have intellect by which you recognize this?

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 68:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They said: "Burn him and support your gods, if you are going to act."﴾ Al-tahriq (burning) is cutting up by means of fire. The scholars differed over who it was who said, "Burn him." On the authority of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, he said: "He was a man from the Kurds of Persia." Others said: "He was Nimrod the tyrant." And on the authority of some of them: "He was a man called Hayrun, whom Allah caused the earth to swallow, and he continues sinking into it until the Day of Resurrection."

As for His words, ﴿and support your gods﴾, al-Azhari said its meaning is: honour your gods by burning him. It was also said: "and defend your gods."

As for His words, ﴿if you are going to act﴾, it means: if you are going to be supporters of them, that is, of the gods.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿We said: "O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham."﴾ In the narrative: they built a furnace (atun) in a village of the villages of Kutha, and they gathered firewood for a period of time. On the authority of al-Suddi, he said: "A man among them would fall ill and would bequeath that firewood be bought and thrown into it, and a woman would spin and buy firewood with her yarn and throw it into it. Then they kindled it for seven days, and then they threw Abraham into it." It is also narrated that they did not know how to throw him into it, so Iblis, may he receive what he deserves, came and taught them how to make the catapult (manjaniq), so they placed him in it and cast him into the fire.

On the authority of Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah al-Muzani, he said: "When Abraham was cast into the fire, all creation cried out and said: 'O Lord, Your intimate friend is being thrown into the fire!' Allah the Exalted said: 'He is My intimate friend; I have no intimate friend other than him, and I am his God; he has no god other than Me. If he seeks help from you, then help him.' But he did not seek help from anyone." It is well known that when he was thrown into the fire he said: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs (hasbiya Allahu wa ni'ma al-wakil)." It is also narrated that he said: "Glory be to You, there is no god but You, Lord of the worlds, and to You be praise, You have no partner." On the authority of Ka'b al-Ahbar and Qatada, they both said: "Everything extinguished the fire from him except the gecko (wizg), for it began blowing on the fire, so the Messenger commanded that it be killed."

And in some reports from the Prophet: "Whoever kills a gecko, it is as though he has killed a disbeliever."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 69:

And His saying: ﴿O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham﴾. That is: possessing coolness. The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: it is possible that He created coolness in the fire in place of heat, and it is possible that He placed a barrier between the fire and Abraham.

And His saying ﴿and safety﴾: it was narrated from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Had He not said ﴿and safety﴾, the coldness would have killed him." A similar report comes from Kaʿb.

And from Qatadah, who said: "Nothing of him was burned except his bonds."

And it is well known in the reports that no one benefited from a fire anywhere in the world on that day.

And His saying: ﴿upon Abraham﴾. Had He not said ﴿upon Abraham﴾, it would have remained coolness forever. In the account: when they threw him into the fire, and Allah made it coolness and safety for him, Nimrod and his companions said: "He has bewitched the fire." Then Abu Lut, who was a disbeliever, said: "Throw another man into it and test it." So they threw another man into it, and the fire consumed him immediately.

And among the strange reports from the Musnads, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "When Abraham was thrown into the fire, Allah sent Gabriel to him, and sent with him a carpet from the carpets of Paradise and a shirt from the shirts of Paradise. He seated him on the carpet, dressed him in the shirt, and sat with him conversing with him." And it was narrated: "They looked, and behold, he was in a garden swaying."

And their saying: ﴿They intended a scheme against him, but We made them the greatest losers.﴾ So the meaning of "the greatest losers" here is that they lost their effort and their expense, and did not attain their aim. Some of them said: its meaning is that God Most High sent gnats upon Nimrod and his people, and they devoured their flesh and drank their blood, and a gnat entered Nimrod's head until it destroyed him. This was related by Muqatil and others.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 21, verse 71:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And We delivered him and Lot to the land which We have blessed for all the worlds﴾. He means: al-Sham (Greater Syria). Its blessing is the abundance of its waters and trees, and the general fertility found in it, so that the poor and the rich live there a good life. It is also said: its blessing is the great number of prophets in it. There is another view regarding this verse: that the intended land which He blessed is Makkah. It is also said: Egypt. But the most correct view is the first, because it is well known that he (Ibrahim) went out with his wife, meaning Ibrahim, to Harran, and then from Harran to al-Sham. As for Lot, he was the son of Ibrahim's brother, and he had gone out with him.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 72:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And We bestowed upon him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The additional gift (nafilah) is Jacob, whereas Isaac is not an additional gift, because God the Exalted granted him Isaac in answer to his supplication, and Jacob was an increase upon what he had asked for. The nafilah is the increase." Mujahid said: "Both of them are a nafilah." The first view is the more sound.

As for His words: ﴿And We made each of them righteous﴾, its meaning is clear.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 73:

And His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And We made them leaders guiding by Our command﴾ means: guiding by Our command.

And His saying: ﴿And We inspired in them the doing of good deeds﴾ means: acting in accordance with the sacred laws (shara'i').

And His saying: ﴿And the establishment of prayer﴾ means: maintaining it (al-muhafaza 'alayha).

﴿And the giving of zakat﴾ means: and giving zakat.

And His saying: ﴿And they were worshippers of Us﴾ means: monotheists (muwahhidun).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 74:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And to Lut We gave judgment and knowledge﴾

And His saying: ﴿And We delivered him from the town that used to commit abominations﴾. The town (al-qarya) is Sodom (Sadum). As for the abominations (al-khaba'ith), it was said: their going in unto males. And it is said that it is: [breaking wind] openly in their assemblies.

And His saying: ﴿Indeed they were a people of evil, defiantly disobedient﴾, the meaning is apparent.
The Almighty's words: ﴿And We admitted him into Our mercy; indeed he was among the righteous.﴾ The meaning is apparent.

The commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 21, verse 76:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Noah, when he called out before[, We answered him]﴾. His calling out was his saying: ﴿Indeed, I am overpowered, so help [me]﴾. (And it was said that it was his saying:) ﴿My Lord, leave not upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant﴾.

And His saying: ﴿So We answered him﴾, meaning: We responded to him.

And His saying: ﴿And We saved him and his people from the great distress﴾. In the narrative: he was the longest-lived of the prophets, and the most severely afflicted of the prophets. It is also related that he used to be beaten seventy times a day.

And His saying: ﴿from the great distress﴾, meaning: from the drowning. It was also said: from grief and constriction.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 77:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We aided him against the people who denied Our signs﴾ — meaning: We protected him and preserved him.

﴿Indeed, they were a people of evil, so We drowned them all﴾ — the meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 78:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And David and Solomon, when they gave judgment concerning the tilth﴾. Scholars differed regarding the tilth (al-harth). Ibn 'Abbas said: it was a vineyard whose clusters had appeared. Qatadah said: it was a field of crops. As for the story concerning it: it is narrated that there were two men, one of whom owned a field and the other owned sheep. The sheep entered the field of his companion at night, ate from it and damaged it, until nothing was left. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿when the flock of the people pastured in it﴾. The nafsh (nafsh) is grazing at night, and the hamal (hamal) is grazing by day. When they woke in the morning, the owner of the field came to dispute with the owner of the sheep before David. David said: "Take the sheep, for they are yours in place of your field." Solomon was there, and he said: "O Prophet of Allah, or is it other than that?" This is the statement of Ibn Mas'ud, that Solomon was present there.

Another said: the two of them went out and passed by Solomon, and mentioned to him the judgment of David. He said: "There was here a judgment that is gentler to the two men." This was reported to his father David, who summoned him and asked him by the right of fatherhood. He said: "The sheep are to be handed over to the owner of the field, to benefit from their milk, their wool and their offspring, and the field is to be handed over to the owner of the sheep to tend it, until it returns to the state it was in on the night the sheep pastured in it, and then the field is to be returned to its owner." This is the meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Solomon﴾. David acted upon this.

As for His saying: ﴿And We were witnesses to their judgment﴾, meaning: their judgment was not hidden from Us in its entirety, and it was by Our knowledge and Our sight.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿So We gave Sulayman the understanding of it﴾. The meaning has already been explained.

The scholars differed over whether Dawud (David) judged by his own *ijtihad* (independent legal reasoning) or by revelation (*wahy*), and likewise Sulayman (Solomon). Some of them said: both of them acted by *ijtihad*. They said: *ijtihad* is permissible for the prophets, so that they may attain the reward of those who exert effort, except that Dawud erred and Sulayman was correct. Error is permissible for the prophets, but they are not left to persist in it. They differed over whether error in judgment is permissible for our Prophet (ﷺ) as it is for the other prophets. Abu 'Ali ibn Abi Hurayra said: it is not permissible, because his law abrogates (*naskh*) the others and there is no prophet after him. Others said: it is permissible, as it is for the other prophets. It has been related that a woman came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "My husband has died, so where should I observe my waiting period?" He said to her: "Observe it wherever you wish." When she turned to leave, he called her back and said: "Glory be to God! Remain in your house until the prescribed term reaches its end." But this report is unusual (*gharib*).

It has also been related that a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, what do you think: if I am killed patiently, seeking reward, will anything prevent me from entering Paradise?" He said: "No." Then he called him back and said: "Except debt; Jibril told me so in secret." This report is well known. The two reports indicate that it is possible for him to err, but he is not left to persist in it.

The second view regarding the basis of the judgment is that Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them, judged by revelation. However, what Dawud judged was abrogated, and what Sulayman judged was abrogating. These people said: it is not permissible for the Prophet to exert *ijtihad* in new cases, because he is independent of *ijtihad* through revelation. God the Exalted has said: ﴿Nor does he speak from desire. It is nothing but revelation revealed﴾. The first view is the more correct.

As for the ruling on this issue in our law: know that what livestock damages at night is guaranteed by its owner, and what it damages by day is not guaranteed. The proof for this is what al-Zuhri related from Haram ibn Muhayyisa, from his father: that the she-camel of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib entered a people's field and damaged it, so they brought the matter before the Prophet (ﷺ), and he ruled that the guarding of livestock at night falls upon its owners, and that the guarding of crops by day falls upon their owners. This is the best ruling possible, because it is the custom that livestock is guarded at night and left to roam by day, whereas crops and produce are guarded by day, and it is difficult to guard them at night.

The Shaykh, the Imam, said: this hadith was related to us by the qadi, the imam, my father, who said: Abu Sahl 'Abd al-Samad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Bazzar narrated to us, who said: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Zakariyya al-Udhari narrated to us, who said: Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Duburi informed us, who said: 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri... the report.

As for His saying: ﴿And to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾, it has already been explained.

If it is said: Dawud had judged by what he judged, and once a judge has given a ruling in a case it is not permissible for it to be overturned by another, so how is this to be understood? The answer is: it is possible that he had been asked to give a judgment and had not yet issued one, but had only stated the basis of the ruling. Others said: he had judged by *ijtihad*, and when Sulayman said what he said, the revelation descended that the judgment was what Sulayman said.

As for His saying: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [God] along with Dawud, and the birds﴾, it was said: their glorification is their prayer. It was also said: their glorification is praising God with purity and sanctification. It has been related that the mountains would respond to Dawud with glorification, and it has been related that when he recited, God let him hear the glorification of the mountains and the birds, so that he would be energized in glorifying and would long for it.

As for His saying: ﴿And We were doers﴾, that is: capable of whatever We will. It was also said that its meaning is: We did what We did through sound planning.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 80:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And We taught him the crafting of armour for you﴾. Al-libas here is the armour (al-dir'), and linguistically al-libas is that which is worn. Qatadah said: "He (Dawud) was the first to weave the armour and to make it with interlocking rings; no one had done so before Dawud. Before him, people would make armour from plates, but when he made the armour, it combined lightness and protection."

And His words: ﴿to protect you from your violence﴾, that is, from the violence of your enemy.

And His words: ﴿to protect you﴾ have been recited in several readings: with the ya', the ta' and the nun. As for the ya', its meaning is: the armour protects you (layuhsinakum al-libas); it was also said: God protects you (layuhsinakum Allah). As for the ta', its meaning is: the craft protects you (latuhsinakum al-san'ah). As for the nun, it refers to God.

And His words: ﴿So will you be grateful?﴾ meaning: O Dawud and the people of his household, will you be grateful?

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 81:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind, blowing forcefully﴾. The stormy wind (al-rih al-'asifa) is that whose blowing is intense. If it is said: He said elsewhere, ﴿gentle, flowing wherever he directed﴾, and "gentle" (al-rakha') means soft? The answer to this is: when he wished it to be intense, it became intense, and when he wished it to be soft, it became soft.

And His words: ﴿flowing by his command toward the land which We had blessed﴾. In the narration: he would travel from al-Sham (Syria) to Istakhr, carried by the wind in the morning, and travel from Istakhr to al-Sham, carried by the wind in the evening.

And His words: ﴿And We were, of all things, knowing﴾. It means: nothing among things was hidden from us.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 82:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And of the devils were those who dived for him﴾. Ghawṣ (diving) is descending into the depths of the sea. The devils would do this for Solomon, to extract pearls and jewels.

And His saying: ﴿and they performed other work besides that﴾, meaning: apart from diving. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿They made for him whatever he willed: sanctuaries, and statues﴾, and so on.

And His saying: ﴿and We were watchful over them﴾.

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said the meaning of this is: We protected the devils from spoiling what they had made. In the story: when Solomon sent a devil with a man to do a task for him, he would say to him: if he finishes his work before nightfall, keep him busy with another task, so that he does not spoil what he has done. It was the habit of the devil that, when he finished a task and was not occupied with another, he would ruin and corrupt what he had done. This is the meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and We were watchful over them﴾, according to what we have mentioned from al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, and it is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 83:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And Ayyub, when he called out to his Lord﴾, meaning: he supplicated his Lord.

And His words: ﴿Indeed, adversity has touched me﴾, meaning: affliction and hardship. It is also said: exertion.

And His words: ﴿And You are the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾, meaning: the Most Merciful of those who show mercy.

Know that the story of Ayyub is long, and the tafsir mentions some of it, and so we too will mention some of it. It is related from al-Hasan al-Basri that Allah the Exalted gave Ayyub wealth and children, then destroyed his wealth and his children. Wahb ibn Munabbih and others mentioned that this was because Iblis was given power over his wealth and children. Al-Hasan said: When the news of the destruction of his wealth and children reached him, he praised Allah abundantly and said: "O Allah, my wealth and my children used to preoccupy me from Your worship, and now my hearing, my sight, my heart, my nights and my days are free for You." Wahb said: Then Allah tested him in his body, and Iblis envied him for his abundant worship and the abundant praise of the people of heaven for him, and said: "O Lord, if You were to test him, he would fall short in Your worship." Allah the Exalted said to him: "I have given you power over his body, except his heart, his tongue and his intellect." This is the statement of Wahb and others, and Allah knows best. Then the affliction appeared in Ayyub's body, and the affliction became extremely severe upon him, until all his body was covered with sores and worms appeared in it. All his people shunned him, and he was cast upon a dunghill of the dunghills of the Children of Israel, and no one approached him except his wife, who used to beg from people and feed him. They differed about the duration of his affliction: Ibn Abbas said seven years, and Wahb said three periods.

As for His words ﴿Indeed, adversity has touched me﴾, the story relates that he did not call upon Allah to remove the harm during that long period until the time of removal arrived, and then he supplicated. They differed about the cause of his supplication. Al-Hasan said: The cause of that was that a group of his friends saw him with that severe affliction, and they said: "If your worship which you used to perform for Allah were sincere, this affliction would not have befallen you." Habib ibn Abi Thabit said: He did not call upon Allah for removal until three things appeared, the most detestable of things. As for the first: two of his friends from Syria came to him when news of him reached them, and they came to him, and nothing of him remained but his eyes, and they saw a great matter, and they said to him: "If you had a station with Allah, this would not have befallen you." The second: his wife asked for food and found nothing to feed him, so she sold her braid and brought him food, and mentioned that to him. The third: when the accursed Iblis saw his patience, he became extremely distressed, so he made a chest, filled it with medicines, and sat on his wife's path treating people. His wife passed by him, and when she saw that, she said: "O man, I have a sick person, may I treat him with you?" He said: "Yes, and I will cure him." She said: "What do you want?" He said: "I want nothing except that when I cure him he says: 'You have cured me.'" She went and mentioned that to Ayyub, peace be upon him, and he said: "It is Iblis who has deceived you. By Allah, if Allah cures me, I will surely strike you a hundred lashes."

It is also related that Iblis came to Ayyub and whispered to him that his wife had committed adultery, and that she had cut her braid for that reason. Then his patience was exhausted because of these things, and he supplicated and said: ﴿Indeed, adversity has touched me﴾.

If someone says: Did not Allah call him patient, and yet he abandoned patience when he supplicated? We say: No, he did not abandon patience, for abandoning patience is by displaying complaint to people; but displaying it to Allah the Exalted is not abandoning patience.

It is related from Sufyan ibn Uyaynah that he said: If one displays complaint to people while being content with the decree of Allah, he is not one who abandons patience either.

It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that Gabriel entered upon him during his final illness and said: "How do you find yourself?" He said: "O Gabriel, I find myself grieved, I find myself distressed."

﴿So We answered him and removed what harm was upon him, and We gave him his family and the like of them with them﴾

It is related that he said to A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her): "Rather, I am, O my head!" The report in full.

In the story: the two worms were fighting over his body, so he would separate them and say to them: "Eat from the provision of Allah."

**Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 84:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So We responded to him and removed the affliction that was upon him.﴾ It is related that God, exalted is He, caused a spring to gush forth for him, and commanded him to bathe in it. He bathed in it and came out in the best condition he could be in.

His saying: ﴿And We gave him his family and the like of them with them.﴾ Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said: his family and his children were returned to him as they were. This is the well-known view, the apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates it, and it is also transmitted through the narration of Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet. In this report it is also mentioned that God returned to his wife her youth, and she bore him twenty-six children after that. In this report also: God sent an angel to him and said: "Indeed your Lord sends you greetings for your patience. Go out to the estates of your threshing floor (andar)." So he went out to them, and God sent upon him locusts of gold. He said: one of them flew off, so he followed it and returned it to his threshing floor. The angel said to him: "Does what is in your threshing floor not suffice you, that you pursue what goes out?" He said: "This is one of the blessings of my Lord; I am never satisfied with His blessing."

The Shaykh, the Imam, said: Abu 'Ali ibn Bandar informed me of this with its chain, from Isma'il ibn Abi Ziyad, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas.

And Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna related, from 'Amr, from Tawus: God rained down upon Ayyub locusts of gold, and he began to gather them in his garment and collect them. It was said to him: "Will you not be satisfied?" He said: "It is from the bounty of my Lord, and I am never satisfied with His bounty." The Shaykh, the Imam, said: Abu 'Ali al-Shafi'i informed me of this, saying: Ibn Firas informed us, saying: al-Dibli informed us, saying: Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Makhzumi informed us, saying: Sufyan informed us, from 'Amr... the report.

There is another view regarding the verse: that the meaning of His saying ﴿And We gave him his family﴾ is the reward of his family, ﴿and the like of them with them﴾ means the like of that, as if his reward was multiplied for him. And from 'Ikrima who said: Ayyub was given the choice between having his family returned to him as they were, or being given the like of his family and children; so he chose that his family be returned to him as they were, and the like of them with them, and he was given that.

His saying: ﴿As a mercy from Us﴾ means: a blessing from Us.

His saying: ﴿And a reminder for the worshippers﴾ means: an admonition and a lesson for the worshippers.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 85:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And Ishmael, and Idris, and Dhu al-Kifl﴾. As for Ishmael and Idris, we have already discussed them. As for Dhu al-Kifl, Ibn 'Abbas said: There was among the Children of Israel a prophet who was also a king. When his death approached, he gathered the Children of Israel and said: "Who will take on for me the responsibility (yakfulu) that he will stand in prayer at night without slackening, that he will fast by day without breaking the fast, and that he will judge with truth and not become angry?" A young man stood up and said: "I will take on that responsibility." So he (the prophet) made him his successor, and that prophet passed away, and he (the young man) fulfilled what he had taken on, and so he was named Dhu al-Kifl (the one who took on the responsibility). Ibn 'Abbas said, in what has been related from him concerning this story: Iblis the accursed, when he saw that, envied him. So he came in the form of a weak old man at midday, and Dhu al-Kifl used to take a nap for a while during his day. He entered upon him and said: "I have a creditor who is delaying me, and I would like you to stand with me and secure my right from him," and he mentioned many words. So he (Dhu al-Kifl) stood up and went out with him. When he had gone out with him for a while, (Iblis) apologized to him and said: "My companion has fled." So Dhu al-Kifl returned, and the time of the midday rest had passed. He (Iblis) did this three days, and he (Dhu al-Kifl) did not see him become angry over any of that, and his sleep had gone during the three days. Then Iblis said to him: "I am Iblis, and I envied you and could not overcome you, and you have fulfilled what you said." This is the well-known opinion.
