There is another view regarding the verse: that Dhu al-Kifl was a man who took on the responsibility of praying one hundred rak'ahs every night until Allah took him, and he fulfilled that, so he was named Dhu al-Kifl. There is disagreement as to whether he was a prophet or not. Some said he was a prophet, and some said he was a righteous servant and not a prophet.

And His saying: ﴿Each of them was among the patient﴾, meaning: patient in obedience to Us.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 21, verse 86:

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And We admitted them into Our mercy﴾. Some of the scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: His saying ﴿And We admitted them into Our mercy﴾ is more eloquent than His saying "and We showed them mercy," because His saying ﴿And We admitted them into Our mercy﴾ implies that they were submerged in mercy, whereas His saying "and We showed them mercy" implies that His mercy reached them.

And His saying ﴿Indeed, they were among the righteous﴾ is clear in meaning, and ṣalāḥ (righteousness) is a term that encompasses all categories of good.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 87:

And the Exalted's saying: ﴿And Dhu'l-Nun, when he went off in anger﴾. Al-Nun: the fish. The poet said:

(Oh, how good is the palace, and how good is the valley... and how good are its people, both settled and nomadic)

(Its pools rise up while the wild beasts graze... and the lizard, the fish (al-nun), the sailor, and the singer)

And His saying: ﴿when he went off in anger﴾. Al-Sha'bi, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: that is, angry with his Lord. As for Ibn 'Abbas, he said: he meant angry with his people. The third view: angry with the king who was in his time.

As for the first view, many scholars disliked it, because whoever is angry with his Lord has committed a great sin. Some of them mentioned that the meaning of "angry with his Lord" is "he opposed his Lord' command." The reason for this is that he promised his people that punishment would come to them on a certain day and then left among them. When that day came and the people of Yunus saw the punishment, they went out and cried out to Allah the Exalted, as we mentioned in the surah of Yunus, and Allah turned the punishment away from them. When it reached Yunus that the punishment had not descended on his people, he became angry. His anger was not out of dislike of God's judgment, but out of dislike of being called a liar. This is the meaning of this view.

﴿and so he thought that We would never have power over him﴾

As for Ibn 'Abbas's view, which is the preferred one, he went off angry with his people when they did not believe. It is sound and correct, with no objection to it.

As for the view of those who said he was angry with the king: 'Ata' al-'Awfi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that there was a king among the Children of Israel who, besides that, was a prophet to whom revelation came. A people had attacked the Children of Israel, so the king summoned Yunus and sent him to those people. Yunus said: "Did God command you to do this, or did He name me for you?" He said: "No, but I am sending you." So he became angry and went out from among them, heading toward the sea.

And His saying: ﴿and so he thought that We would never have power over him﴾. Ibn 'Abbas recited: "fa-zanna an lan naqdira 'alayh," which is irregular. Ibn 'Amir recited: "fa-zanna an lan naqdira 'alayh." Know that in this verse there is a well-known question, counted among the difficulties of the Qur'an: how could he think this about Allah, and whoever thinks this about Allah has disbelieved? The answer: the verse has two meanings. The first: the meaning of His saying ﴿and so he thought that We would never have power over him﴾ is "We would never decree over him," in the sense of judgment and decree. It is said: qadara and qadara have the same meaning, except that one says yaqdiru (qadara, to decree/measure) and yuqaddiru (qaddara, to decree/measure with emphasis). The poet said:

(Those evenings at al-Liwa will never return to us, as long as the fresh spring rain pours down)

(Nor will that time that has passed return. Blessed are You; whatever You decree comes to pass, and to You belongs thanks)

That is: "yuqaddiruhu" (decrees it).

From this is His saying: "If the sky is overcast for you, then estimate it" (i.e., decree it for it), which is a sound report.

The second meaning of the answer: the meaning of His saying ﴿and so he thought that We would never have power over him﴾ is "We would never constrict him." From this is the Exalted's saying: ﴿And as for when He tries him and restricts his provision﴾, meaning constricts it. Know that the meaning of constriction and restriction upon him is confinement in the belly of the fish.

The people of knowledge said: Yunus was not one of the prophets of resolute purpose (ulu al-'azm), and he had a constricted breast. When the burdens of prophethood were placed upon him, he buckled under them as a rope buckles under a load. This view is transmitted from the early generations (al-salaf).

And His saying: ﴿So he called out in the darknesses﴾. In the narrative: when he boarded the ship, there were many people in the ship. A fish came and held the ship back, and the people feared destruction for themselves. Yunus realized that he was the one intended and said: "Throw me overboard and you will be saved." They refused to do so. Then they cast lots, and the lot fell upon him several times, so they threw him, and the fish swallowed him, and the ship went on. Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd said: another fish swallowed the fish.

As for His saying ﴿So he called out in the darknesses﴾: that is, the darkness of the night, the darkness of the sea, and the darkness of the belly of the fish. In the narrative: the fish carried him down to the seventh earth, and he heard from the glorification of the earths, the stones, and the creatures of the seas a tremendous matter, so he called out in the darknesses: ﴿There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: he remained in it forty days. According to another: three days. It is reported that when he made this supplication, the angels heard his voice and said: "O Lord, a known voice from an unknown place!" Allah the Exalted said: "It is My servant Yunus. I made the belly of the fish a prison for him, so they supplicated."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 88:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So We answered him﴾, meaning: We responded to him.

And His saying: ﴿and We delivered him from the distress﴾, that is: from the distress of the sea and the narrowness of the place.

And His saying: ﴿And thus do We deliver the believers﴾. It has been recited as "najja l-mu'minin" (with a single nun and a doubled jim, as in "najja"), but the preferable reading is with two nuns. Al-Zajjaj said: "With a single nun is a solecism (lahn), and it is an error (min al-khata'), which 'Asim related from him."

It is narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "There is a word I know that no one says in a time of distress except that relief comes from it, and it is the word of my brother Yunus: 'There is no god but You, glory be to You, indeed I have been among the wrongdoers.'"

In the narrative: the fish cast him onto the shore of the sea, and Allah caused a gourd plant (shajara min yaqtin) to grow for him. The account of this will come later in Surat al-Saffat. If it is said: His saying ﴿And thus do We deliver the believers﴾ is written in the Mushaf with a single nun, so how did you make the more correct of the two readings the one with two nuns? The answer to this: it was written with a single nun only because the first nun is vowelled (mutaharrika) and the second nun is unvowelled (sakina), so the unvowelled one was obscured beside the vowelled one and was dropped. Al-Farra' has mentioned an interpretation of the reading of 'Asim, namely that its meaning is: "the deliverance (al-najja'") delivered the believers," so "al-mu'minin" is in the genitive case (khufida) by the supposition of an omitted verbal noun (idmar al-masdar).

Almost all of Zakariyya's supplication is here, so I'll translate faithfully.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Zakariyya, when he called out to his Lord﴾ means: he invoked his Lord.

And His saying: ﴿My Lord, do not leave me alone (fardan)﴾ means: solitary, without an heir. Its meaning is what we mentioned of the supplication for a child.

And His saying: ﴿and You are the best of inheritors﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 90:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So We answered him﴾, meaning: So We responded to him.

As for His saying: ﴿And We gave him Yahya﴾, he was named Yahya because his mother's womb was made alive (ḥayy) by the child.

As for His saying: ﴿And We made his wife fit for him﴾, there are two views. The first, which is the well-known one, is that she was barren and He made her fertile. The second is what has been transmitted from ʿAṭāʾ, that he said: the meaning of "making fit" (iṣlāḥ) is that there was length of tongue in his wife and bad character in her, so He made her good.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds﴾ refers to all the prophets he mentioned.

His saying: ﴿they used to hasten﴾, meaning: they would race to do them.

His saying: ﴿And they called upon Us in hope and in fear﴾, meaning: in hope of obedience (to be rewarded) and in fear of sins (to be spared). (It was said: in hope of Paradise and in fear of the Fire.) Khuṣayf said: "In hope, with the palms turned down; in fear, with them turned up."

His saying: ﴿And they were humbly submissive to Us﴾, meaning: humble. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: it is that one places his right hand upon his left in prayer, and directs his gaze to the place of prostration. Mujāhid said: khushūʿ is the fear that is constant in the heart. It is related from al-Ḥasan that he said: "Submissive to the command of Allah, Exalted is He."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 91:

﴿And she who guarded her chastity﴾, that is, she kept her private part chaste; and it is said: she refrained from what is forbidden.

As for His saying: ﴿So We breathed into her of Our Spirit﴾, most of the scholars hold that this refers to the opening of her shirt (jayb al-dir', the collar of the garment), as we have explained. There is another view: that He breathed into her womb, and God created the Messiah in her belly. He mentioned "Our Spirit" as a specification and an honour for the Messiah, peace be upon him.

As for His saying: ﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾.

That is, a proof for the worlds. If it is said: "They were two signs, so why did He not say 'two signs'?" The answer is: He said "a sign" because the sign in them was one, namely that she brought him forth without a male (fahl, a stallion/male partner). The scholars of knowledge said: and in it there are several signs. The first: that no woman before her had been impregnated in order to be guarded (against it). The second: her bringing forth 'Isa without a father. The third: the coming of her provision from God without any cause from a created being. And it is said: he did not take the breast of anyone except his mother.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 92:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community﴾, meaning: your religion (milla) and your faith (din) are one religion (milla). In the original linguistic sense, "umma" (community) is a name for a group, and the religion was called "umma" because it prompts gathering together (ijtima').

And His saying: ﴿And I am your Lord, so worship Me﴾, meaning: make Me one (wahhidunī), i.e., affirm My oneness. The true meaning of the verse is that the religion to which I have called you is the religion of the prophets before you, since the religion of all of them is one. This refers to tawhid (monotheism). As for the sacred laws (shara'i'), their differing is permissible. It is also said: the meaning of the verse is that you are one creation, so be upon one religion.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 93:

The words of God, the Exalted: ﴿And they cut their affair into pieces among themselves﴾. That is: I called the creation to one religion, but they scattered. It is also said: they became fragments, dispersed.

And His words: ﴿To Us they will all return﴾. That is: whether they scattered or did not scatter.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 94:

The words of the Most High: ﴿So whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer, there will be no denial of his effort﴾. That is: there will be no rejection of his effort. It is also said: his effort will not be lost, but he will be rewarded for it.

And His words: ﴿Indeed, We record it for him﴾. That is: We preserve it. It is also said that the meaning of gratitude (shukr) from Allah is recompense.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 95:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there is a prohibition upon a town﴾ (wa-ḥarām ʿalā qaryatin). It is also recited as "wa-ḥaram." Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning of His saying ﴿ḥarām﴾ is "obligatory" (wājib). The poet said:

(And indeed, I do not see that I will ever weep for a ḥarām [obligatory] matter over a mourning-remnant (shajwa) except that I weep over ʿAmr.)

That is, "obligatory." So the meaning of the verse according to this is: it is obligatory upon a town that We have destroyed that they will not return to the world. If it is said: how can He make it obligatory upon them that they not return, when they are not subject to obligation, permission, or anything else?

The answer: this is an extension of speech (tawassuʿ al-kalām), and its meaning is that We prevent them from returning. Prohibition (taḥrīm) in the language is precisely prevention (manʿ).

The second view: "lā" is extra (ṣila), as stated by Abu ʿUbayd. Its meaning is: prohibited upon a town that We have destroyed, that they return. Al-Zajjaj said: His saying ﴿And there is a prohibition upon a town﴾ means: and there is a prohibition upon the people of a town ﴿that We have destroyed﴾, i.e., We have decreed its destruction, that their deeds be accepted, because ﴿they do not return﴾, i.e., they do not turn back. He said: the evidence for this meaning is that He said in the verse before it: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer, then there is no denial of his effort﴾, i.e., his deed is accepted. Then He mentioned after it this verse, clarifying that the disbeliever's deed is not accepted.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 96:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Until, when Gog and Magog are let loose﴾ are recited with both the light and the intensive (tashdid) forms. The intensive form means the plural, and the light form means the singular.

And His words: ﴿Gog and Magog﴾ have already been explained. The "opening" refers to the barrier that stands between us and them. It is said that creation consists of ten parts: nine parts are all Gog and Magog, and one part is the rest of creation. It is also said that one part out of a thousand is the rest of creation, and the remainder are Gog and Magog.

His words: ﴿and they will come swarming down from every mound﴾. The "hadab" (mound) is an elevated place, so its meaning is that they hasten down from the hills, and it is an elevated place of the fortresses. The "nasalan" of the wolf is the speed of its walking. The poet said:

(The wolf's swift gait, when it grew evident, / with the cold of the night upon it, it sped along.)

It is also said: "from every hadab" means from every side. If it is asked: what is the meaning of "until" (hatta) at the beginning of the verse, and where is its response? The answer: some of them said its meaning is: "until, when Gog and Magog are let loose and they come swarming down from every mound, the true promise draws near," and the waw is superfluous (muqhamah). Imru' al-Qays said:

(So when we passed the courtyard of the tribe and it veered / with us toward the valley of Khabt, with its winding dunes.)

The waw in his words "wa-intaha" is superfluous.

The second view: the meaning of His words, "until, when Gog and Magog are let loose and they come swarming down from every mound," is that they say, ﴿Woe to us!﴾. It is also said that the truth of what we have said becomes manifest to them. And in some strange reports, through the narration of Ibn Mas'ud: "The Prophet (ﷺ), on the night he was taken on the Night Journey, gathered with Abraham, Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them. They mentioned the matter of the Hour, and they began with Abraham and asked him about it. He said: 'I have no knowledge of it.' Then they mentioned it to Moses, and he said: 'I have no knowledge of it.' Then they mentioned it to Jesus, and Jesus said: 'Allah the Exalted has charged me that its time is hidden, and none knows its knowledge except Allah.' Then Jesus said: 'Allah will send me down to the earth, and I will kill the Dajjal.'"

A report has come: "Gog and Magog will have come forth and will overpower the earth. Then the Muslims will cry out to Allah, and Allah will send the nagf (a worm) into their necks, and they will perish. The earth will stink from them; then Allah will send birds like the necks of Bukht camels, which will seize them and cast them into the sea."

And from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "People will perform Hajj and 'umrah after the emergence of Gog and Magog and their destruction."

The Exalted saying: ﴿And the true promise has drawn near﴾. We have already explained it.

And His saying: ﴿Then behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved will be fixed in horror﴾, meaning: alarmed.

And His saying: ﴿They will say, "Woe to us! We were certainly heedless of this; rather, we were wrongdoers"﴾. Its meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 98:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾. ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) read "ḥaṭab Jahannam" (ḥaṭab, firewood), and al-Jaḥdarī read "ḥaṣab Jahannam" (ḥaṣab, fuel). There is also in the irregular readings (shādhdh): "ḥaḍab Jahannam," with the letter ḍād pointed and vowelled. As for the well-known reading, ﴿ḥaṣab Jahannam﴾, it refers to that which is thrown into the Fire.

As for His saying, ﴿and what you worship besides Allah﴾: it is related that when the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse to the disbelievers, ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Zibaʿrā said: "I have bested Muḥammad, by the Lord of the Kaʿbah!" Then he said: "O Muḥammad, do you claim that whatever is worshipped besides Allah will enter the Fire?" He said: "Yes." (And al-Wurūd here means: entering.) Ibn al-Zibaʿrā said: "Then ʿĪsā, ʿUzayr and the angels are worshipped besides Allah; will they be in the Fire with us?" Then Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the good reward from Us has preceded, they will be kept far from it﴾. Allah also revealed concerning ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Zibaʿrā: ﴿They do not strike this example for you except for argument. Rather, they are a quarrelsome people﴾. The meaning is that they said what they said out of contentiousness and disputation based on falsehood, for they certainly knew that what was intended were the idols.

Qaṭrab (Qaṭrib) and a group of grammarians claimed that the verse, from the standpoint of Arabic, applies only to the idols, because Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and what you worship besides Allah﴾, and this (the particle mā) is used for that which does not reason. As for those who reason, one says: "And whom do you worship besides Allah?"

Almighty Allah's saying: ﴿If these were gods, they would not have entered it﴾, i.e., they would not have entered it.

And His saying: ﴿and all in it will abide eternally﴾, i.e., they will remain.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 100:

The Most High's words: ﴿For them therein is groaning (zafir)﴾. We have already explained the meaning of zafir.

And His words: ﴿And they therein will not hear﴾.

Ibn Mas'ud said: They will be placed in coffins of fire. Some of them said: And the coffins are within coffins, so they hear nothing and see nothing, and each one thinks that no one else is being punished, so that he will have no consolation in the example (of others). And this report is not from the words of Ibn Mas'ud.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 101:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has preceded from Us﴾ has already been explained.

It is also said: the happiness (sa'ada) preceded for them from Us. It is also said: Paradise became obligatory for them.

His saying: ﴿those will be kept far away from it﴾ — its meaning is apparent.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿They will not hear its faintest sound﴾, meaning: its ḥas (حس), that is, its sound.

And His words: ﴿And they will abide in what their souls desire, dwelling eternally﴾, meaning: they will remain (مقيمون, muqīmūn).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 103:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "The greatest terror is that Hell will be closed over them, and that is after Allah has brought out of it whoever He wills to bring out." It is also said: "The greatest terror is the slaughtering of death, so it will be said to these: eternity without death, and to those: eternity without death." It is also said: "The greatest terror is the command to be dragged to the Fire."

His saying: ﴿And the angels will receive them﴾, meaning: the angels will meet them.

His saying: ﴿This is your day which you were promised﴾, the meaning is clear.

The Exalted said: ﴿On the Day We roll up the heaven like the rolling of a scroll for writings.﴾ It has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah will fold up the heavens, and He will take the earth in His right hand and say: I am the King; where are the kings of the earth?"

As for His words: ﴿like the rolling of a scroll for writings﴾, it is narrated from Ibn Ishaq that "the scroll" was a scribe of the Prophet (ﷺ), but this is a strange view. The second view is that "the scroll" is an angel. The third view, which is the most correct of the views, is that "the scroll" is the page.

As for His words: ﴿for writings﴾, meaning: because of what is written. So its meaning is: like the rolling of the page because of what is written on it.

As for His words: ﴿As We began the first creation, We shall repeat it﴾, meaning: Our power to recreate creation is like Our power to originate it.

As for His words: ﴿Indeed, We are ever doers﴾, meaning: able to do it. In regard to this verse, a sound report has come, which is what Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from Ibn Abbas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection barefoot, naked and uncircumcised." In another narration: "Indeed you will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection barefoot, naked and uncircumcised," then he recited: ﴿As We began the first creation, We shall repeat it﴾. "The first to be clothed will be Abraham, peace be upon him. Then some people from my community will be brought, and they will be commanded toward the Fire. I will say: O Lord, my companions! He will say: Indeed, they have not ceased to turn back on their heels since you parted from them. So I will say as the righteous servant said: ﴿And I was a witness over them as long as I was among them; but when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them, and You are Witness over all things.﴾" In another narration: "I will say: Away, away with the people of the Fire." The Shaykh, the Imam said: I was informed of this hadith by al-Makki ibn Abd al-Razzaq, who said: my grandfather Abu al-Haytham informed us, who said: al-Firabri said: al-Bukhari said: Muhammad ibn Kathir narrated to us, from Sufyan al-Thawri, from al-Mughirah ibn al-Nu'man, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr... the report.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 105:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We had written in the Zabur after the Dhikr﴾. ʿĀmir ibn Sharahil al-Shaʿbi, Abu ʿAmr, said: the Zabur is the Zabur of Dawud, and the Dhikr is the Tawrah (the Torah). Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: the Zabur is the Torah and the Injil, and the Dhikr is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), and its meaning is: after its mention had been written in the Preserved Tablet.

And His saying: ﴿that the earth, My righteous servants will inherit it﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the earth is the land of Paradise. And from him also: the earth is the lands of the disbelievers, which Allah will open to the Muslims and make theirs. It was also said: the earth is the Holy Land (al-Ard al-Muqaddasah).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 106:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, in this is a message (balaghan)﴾. It is permissible that His saying, ﴿in this﴾, means in the Qur'an, and it is permissible that its meaning is: in this surah. His saying, ﴿a message﴾, means a means that conveys them to the pleasure of Allah. It was also said: balaghan means sufficiency.

And His saying, ﴿for a people who worship﴾. It was said: "who know" (ʿalimin), and it was said: "who obey" (muti'in).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 107:

Allah's saying, ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾, is among the well-known and established matters transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "I am only a mercy given as a gift" (rahma muhdah), meaning: a gift from Allah.

Then the scholars differed concerning "the worlds" (al-'alamin) on two views. One view is that they are the Muslims, so he is a mercy to the Muslims. The second view is that they are all of creation, and this view is more widely known. As for the meaning of his mercy to the disbelievers, it is the postponement of punishment from them. It was also said that it is the lifting of the punishment of annihilation (adhab al-isti'sal) from them. As for his mercy to the believers, it is well known.
Almighty God's words: ﴿Say: It is only revealed to me that your God is one God. Will you then submit?﴾ That is, submit (aslimu).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 109:

His saying: ﴿So if they turn away, then say: I have announced to you on equal terms﴾ means: so that you may be equal in belief in it. The most evident of the opinions is what Ibn Qutaybah mentioned, that its meaning is: I have announced to you in a manner in which we and you are equal in knowledge of it.

And His saying: ﴿And I do not know whether it is near or far﴾ means: I do not know whether what you are promised (ma tu'adun) is near or far.
His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, He knows what is spoken aloud﴾ the verse? . The meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 111:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And I do not know, perhaps it is a trial for you﴾. The scholars differed over what the pronoun in ﴿perhaps﴾ (la'allahu) refers back to, on two views. The first: it refers to His saying, ﴿And I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far﴾, meaning: this which I say may be a trial for you. The second view: it refers to what we have mentioned, namely the delay of the punishment from them. And His saying ﴿a trial﴾ means a test and an examination.

And His saying ﴿and an enjoyment for a time﴾ means until the Resurrection; it was also said: until death.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 21, verse 112:

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿Say: "My Lord, judge with truth."﴾ Ḥafs, on the authority of ʿĀṣim, recited: "He said: 'My Lord, judge with truth,'" in the form of a report (khabar). The first reading is the preferred one. Moreover, the consonantal text of the muṣḥaf (sawād al-muṣḥaf) is to be followed, and it is not permissible to oppose it.

If it is asked: how is this supplication (duʿāʾ) permissible, given that God judges only with truth? The answer: we say that it is related from Qatādah that he said: "The prophets before Muḥammad used to say: 'Our Lord, decide between us and our people with truth,' so God commanded His Messenger to say: 'My Lord, judge with truth.'"

They differed about its meaning. Some of them said: "My Lord, judge with truth" means: hasten the judgment with truth. Abū ʿUbayd said: "My Lord, judge by Your true judgment." God judges with truth whether or not He is asked. The meaning of "asking" (ṭalab) is the manifestation of the petitioner's desire for His judgment to be with truth. This last explanation is not from the statement of Abū ʿUbayda. Some of them said: ﴿My Lord, judge with truth﴾ is an act of worship (taʿabbud) from God, and God judges with truth whether or not He is asked; this was cited by al-Naḥḥās.

His statement: ﴿And our Lord, the Most Merciful, is the One sought for help against what you describe.﴾ That is: against what you lie about. Similar to this is His statement, the Exalted: ﴿He will repay them for their description﴾, that is, He will repay them for their lying. It is also said: "against what you describe" means: what you lie about.
